blogs.title: Gender Issues: Understanding Gender and Society
blogs.excerpt: Gender shapes expectations, access, safety, and opportunity across education, work, media, and identity. Understanding these dynamics helps build a more just and compassionate society for everyone.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
Understanding Gender and Society

Gender is one of the first labels assigned to us. Before we speak our first word, before we take our first step, our society begins shaping expectations around who we are supposed to be. From the colours we wear, to the careers we choose. Gender influences not only how others perceive us but also how we perceive ourselves.

While progress has been made over the past couple of years to address inequality, gender issues remain deeply rooted in our social structures, cultural norms and personal experiences.

Understanding gender issues is not about creating a comparison between men and women. It is about recognizing how rigid expectations, unequal opportunities and systemic biases affect people differently in various aspects of life and how we can work together to build a more just and compassionate society.

## Sex vs. Gender: The Difference

Before we move further, we must understand the terms to get a better insight. Many people use the terms sex and gender interchangeably but they are not the same.

Biological sex refers to physical characteristics such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy of an individual. On the other hand, gender is a social and cultural construct. It involves roles, behaviours, expectations and identities that societies assign to each individual.

For centuries, societies operated within a binary framework male and female, assigning strict roles to each. Men were often expected to be strong, dominant and financially responsible, while women were expected to be nurturing, emotional and primarily responsible for domestic work.

These roles may have provided structure in traditional societies but they also limited individual freedom and potential.

## Barriers to Growth: Education and Workplace Inequality

One of the most visible gender issues worldwide is inequality in access to education and employment opportunities.

In many parts of the world, girls still face problems in schools due to poverty, cultural norms, lack of sanitation facilities, early marriage or safety concerns. Without education, their opportunities to achieve financial independence reduce dramatically.

Even in societies where women have access to education, workplace inequality persists. The gender pay gap remains one of the persisting global issues, with women often earning less than men for similar roles and responsibilities.

Be it leadership positions in politics, business, arts or science, they are still dominated by men.

At the same time, gender expectations also harm men. Many boys grow up being told not to cry, not to show vulnerability and to equate masculinity with emotional suppression. This pressure can lead to mental health struggles that often go unaddressed for years.

## Gender-Based Violence: A Global Concern

Gender based violence is one of the most serious and urgent issues globally.

Women and girls are affected by domestic violence, harassment and sexual assault. Fear of violence often restricts freedom, influencing where someone feels safe to travel, what they wear and how they behave in public.

Addressing gender based violence requires more than laws. It demands cultural change, teaching respect, consent and equality from an early age.

Similarly, men can also be victims of violence, though societal stigma often prevents them from speaking up. Breaking the silence around these issues is essential for true gender justice.

## Media and Reinforcement of Gender Norms

The media plays a powerful role in shaping gender norms. Movies, advertisements, music and social media frequently reinforce stereotypes where women may be portrayed primarily through their appearance, while men are portrayed as powerful decision-makers.

Such portrayals subtly influence how young people see themselves and what they believe they are capable of achieving.

There is no doubt the media also has the power to challenge stereotypes. Stories that depict women as leaders, men as caregivers and individuals expressing diverse gender identities help normalize a broader spectrum of human experience.

Representation matters because it expands the horizon.

## Gender Identity and Evolving Conversations

In the past couple of years, conversations about gender identity have become more visible. Some individuals do not identify strictly as male or female. For them, rigid gender systems can be restrictive and harmful.

While perspectives on gender identity can vary across cultures and belief systems, one principle remains universal: every human being deserves dignity and respect.

Regardless of personal views, fostering dialogue grounded in empathy rather than hostility creates healthier communities.

Gender issues are not always dramatic or headline-making. Sometimes they are subtle in everyday conversations, expectations and experiences.

Why are girls often praised for being quiet and well-behaved, while boys are excused for being naturally mischievous? Why are women asked about balancing family and career in interviews more frequently than men? Why is caregiving still primarily seen as a woman’s responsibility?

These are small biases that have built over time. They influence confidence, ambition and opportunity. Challenging them requires awareness and highlighting that such assumptions are based not on ability, but on gender.

## Towards an Equal Society

Real change begins with education. Schools, families and communities play a critical role in shaping perspectives. Teaching young people about equality, mutual respect and shared responsibility lays the foundation for a more balanced society.

Open conversations are equally important. When people share experiences we must listen actively and seek understanding rather than argue. Through dialogue growth becomes possible.

Gender equality is not a women’s issue or a men’s issue. It is a human issue.

Gender issues are complex, deeply rooted and interconnected with culture, economics, religion and history. But at their core, they revolve around one simple principle: being just.

When individuals are free to pursue education, careers, relationships and self-expression without being limited by rigid expectations, society as a whole benefits. Innovation increases, families grow healthier, and communities become stronger.

Addressing gender issues is not about replacing one dominance with another. It is about balance, recognizing the value, dignity and potential of every person.

blogs.title: Women and Equity in AI Technology
blogs.excerpt: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping economies and societies. This piece examines equity in AI, the gendered digital divide, and the steps needed to build inclusive, safe, and fair technology systems.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
The world finds itself at the threshold of the Fourth Industrial Revolution characterised by [velocity, scope, and systems impact.](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2016/01/the-fourth-industrial-revolution-what-it-means-and-how-to-respond/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=22228224717&gbraid=0AAAAAoVy5F4vZIO7zLrAjqdSREJe1x4RT&gclid=CjwKCAiA-__MBhAKEiwASBmsBDIHKgRbK5Sgbmo3ilKggSp2rKafgDVKqLnQmw-_zIZdAAE8eY3gGBoCXTsQAvD_BwE) Technological innovations are changing the world as we know it faster than ever before. Emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, robotics, 3-D printing, nanotechnology, biotechnology and quantum computing, etc. are changing the rules of businesses and societies. What does it mean for the women in those businesses and societies?

## Equity in Technological Solutions

Equity in technology can be defined as [intentional design, development, deployment, and governance of technology systems](https://climate.sustainability-directory.com/term/equity-in-technology/) to ensure values such as justice, fairness and inclusion for all.

The percentage of women in STEM is a matter of concern. Women have far less access and digital literacy as compared to men. There are [only 35 per cent of students in STEM education.](https://www.un.org/en/un75/impact-digital-technologies) There are [only 22 per cent of jobs in the artificial intelligence (AI) arena.](https://www.un.org/en/un75/impact-digital-technologies) During conception, when a technology is shaped under a narrow perspective, it negatively affects inclusiveness. [OECD found that,](https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/gender-equality-and-digital-transformation.html#:~:text=Human%20capital%20is%20required%20to,encouraged%20to%20undertake%20STEM%20studies.) male bias in ICT reduces the inclusiveness in digital transformation. It also found that while the exposure to AI remains the same for both males and females in their occupations, women are significantly under-represented in occupations that have the highest exposure to AI technology.

## Barriers- Gatekeeping of Technology?

A major barrier to inclusion of women in technology related fields are gender based digital divide, early age discouragement and stereotyping of job roles, limited role models in STEM, [lack of mentorship,](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) gender bias and [discrimination in hiring](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) and [an unwelcoming and hostile environment for women](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) in technology spaces. These factors inhibit women from being part of the workforce in technology related fields.

## What Next?

Attention must be redirected to the consequences of the Fourth Industrial Revolution on people and more specifically on women. A major dissuader of the usage of technology is the possible abuse and harassment on digital platforms; therefore, it is imperative to ensure safety on these platforms. Enforcing strict laws to ensure privacy and timely action against harassment along with providing digital literacy to women can foster a safer digital environment for women.

Focus needs to be drawn upon the unequal access to technology due to barriers such as income, education, region, social status, etc. Addressing these differences is key to bringing change. One way to address this is by reexamining existing knowledge about technology as a government provided public good. Governments must ensure an [inclusive approach in skilling](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2024/12/algorithm-and-eve_0e889c45/full-report.html#a1zLan24) women in artificial intelligence technology.

It is also the need of the hour to promote inclusion of women in the field of STEM and in workplaces with high AI exposure. Mandating diversity in hiring and promoting skills-first approach in hiring and other targeted approaches can address discrimination in hiring. Awareness campaigns can be run to illustrate the importance of access to technology to women. With these changes there can be significant progress in achieving equity in the AI workforce.
